mainTopic: How many people read the Torah on different days, and the laws and stories about bowing down (נפילת אפים, קידה, השתחואה)
overview: The גמרא first finishes rejecting a proof from a story about רב about how many people read from the Torah on a תענית ציבור. It then brings a ברייתא that settles the question: on days when a long service keeps people from work, such as a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב, three read. On ראש חודש and חול המועד, four read. רב אשי objects that the כלל of our משנה seems to add fast days to the four-reader group. The גמרא answers that his reading fits no known תנא, since even the ברייתא about תשעה באב allows at most three readers. It then explains that the כלל is only a סימן: each step up in a day's importance adds one reader, which gives four for ראש חודש and מועד, five for יום טוב, six for יום הכפורים, and seven for שבת. Next the גמרא goes back to the story of רב, who did not fall on his face on a fast day, and gives three explanations: the stone floor, his custom of bowing fully stretched out, and the rule that an important person should not fall on his face in public. A ברייתא then defines קידה, כריעה and השתחואה. A story follows about לוי, who was injured demonstrating קידה. The amud ends as רב חייא בר אבין begins describing how אביי bowed, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: People would not walk out on רב
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the rejection of the proof from the story of רב. Since nobody would leave early while רב was present, his skipping the closing ברכה tells us nothing about how many people read.
steps.simpleTranslation: They would not leave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its rejection of the earlier attempt to prove, from the story of רב, how many read on a fast day. It says that with רב present, people simply would not leave early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The closing ברכה after the last reader was instituted for people who leave the בית כנסת after the reading. רב skipped it, so the proof argued that he was not the last reader, which would mean more readers came after him. This line answers that even if רב was the last reader, nobody would walk out in front of him, so the closing ברכה was not needed. His behavior therefore does not prove how many people read, and the proof from the story falls away.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is the tail end of an argument from the previous section. On its own it looks like a random fact. Its job is to knock down the proof from the story of רב.

phrases.english: As for leaving, they would not leave.
phrases.notes: Out of respect for רב, the people would not walk out early, so the closing ברכה was not needed to signal anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the rejection of the proof from the story of רב, which began on the previous amud.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the attempt to learn the number of readers on a תענית ציבור from how רב handled the ברכות.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב's special status explains his behavior (no one would leave in his presence), so his actions do not show how many people read.

steps.title: A ברייתא: three read on fast days, four on ראש חודש and חול המועד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a general rule. Days when a longer service would keep people from work, such as a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב, have three readers. Days without that concern, such as ראש חודש and חול המועד, have four readers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: This is the rule. Any day on which there is a loss of work for the people, such as a public fast day and the Ninth of Av, three people read. Any day on which there is no loss of work for the people, such as the New Moon and the intermediate days of a Festival, four people read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof by quoting a ברייתא that openly states how many read on a fast day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא bases the number of readers on ביטול מלאכה, meaning how much a longer service would take people away from their work. On a fast day people are allowed to work, so the reading is kept short with three readers. On ראש חודש (when women customarily refrain from work) and on חול המועד (when work is restricted anyway), adding a fourth reader costs nobody anything.

keyTerms.meaning: come and hear: introduces a source brought as proof
the intermediate days of a Festival

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא offers a new reason for the number of readers: whether people lose work time. That is a different kind of reason from the extra-holiness standard (מוסף, יום טוב) used in our משנה.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
phrases.notes: This is how the גמרא brings in a source to prove its point.

phrases.english: This is the general rule:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ בִּיטּוּל מְלָאכָה לָעָם,
phrases.english: Any day on which there is a loss of work for the people,
phrases.notes: A longer service would keep people from work they are allowed to do.

phrases.english: for example, a public fast day and the Ninth of Av,
three people read.
phrases.notes: Kept short so as not to hold people back from work.

phrases.english: And any day on which there is no loss of work for the people,

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן רָאשֵׁי חֳדָשִׁים וְחוּלּוֹ שֶׁל מוֹעֵד —
phrases.english: for example, the New Moon and the intermediate days of a Festival,
phrases.notes: On ראש חודש women customarily refrain from work; on חול המועד work is restricted.

phrases.english: four people read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from רב is rejected, the גמרא brings a new proof from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That on a תענית ציבור only three people read from the Torah.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that sorts days by ביטול מלאכה and explicitly gives three readers for a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב.

steps.title: Conclusion: three read on a fast day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the ברייתא's proof: on a תענית ציבור, three people read.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the proof works: we now know that three people read on a fast day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the ברייתא names a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב outright, there is nothing to push back on. The question that began the discussion seems settled, though רב אשי is about to challenge it.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from this: the proof is accepted

phrases.english: Learn from this.
phrases.notes: Meaning: on a public fast day, three people read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: On a תענית ציבור and on תשעה באב, three people read from the Torah.

steps.title: רב אשי cites the כלל of our own משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי objects by quoting the general rule of our משנה: any day that has a מוסף but is not a יום טוב has four readers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: But didn't we learn in our משנה as follows: This is the rule: any day on which there is an additional offering and it is not a Festival, four people read.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי begins a challenge by quoting the summary rule at the end of our משנה. This step sets up the next move, where he will show what that rule must be including.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה already lists ראש חודש and חול המועד by name as days with four readers. It then adds a כלל. A כלל written after a list usually comes to include something more, and רב אשי is about to say what that is.

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't we ourselves learn (in the משנה)?
an additional offering or additional prayer

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
But didn't we learn in our Mishnah as follows:
This is the general rule:
any day on which there is an additional offering
phrases.notes: רב אשי will read 'מוסף' broadly enough to cover an addition to the prayers on a fast day.

phrases.english: and it is not a Festival,
four people read.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי, וְהָא אֲנַן לָא תְּנַן הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion just reached by setting our משנה against the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that three people read on a תענית ציבור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our משנה's general rule seems to call for four readers on any non-יום טוב day that has an addition, which would include fast days.

steps.title: The כלל must be including fast days
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי argues that the כלל of the משנה must come to include a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב. That would mean four people read on them, the opposite of the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does the rule come to include? Doesn't it come to include a public fast day and the Ninth of Av?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks what extra case the משנה's כלל adds. He answers that it must be fast days, which would put them in the four-reader group.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ראש חודש and חול המועד are already listed by name, so the כלל must be adding something else. On a fast day there is an addition to the prayers (עננו), so רב אשי reads it as the 'מוסף' of the כלל. That makes the משנה say four readers on a fast day, which clashes with the ברייתא's three.

keyTerms.meaning: what does this come to include?
is it not? (introduces the expected answer)

steps.confusionAlert: A fast day has no מוסף offering in the מקדש. רב אשי is reading 'מוסף' in the משנה broadly, to mean any addition to the day's prayers.
steps.whatToRemember: There is now a clash. The ברייתא says three read on a fast day, while רב אשי reads our משנה's כלל as saying four.

phrases.english: What does it come to include?
phrases.notes: ראש חודש and חול המועד are already stated, so the כלל must add something new.

phrases.aramaic: לָאו לְאֵתוֹיֵי תַּעֲנִית צִיבּוּר וְתִשְׁעָה בְּאָב!
phrases.english: Doesn't it come to include a public fast day and the Ninth of Av!
phrases.notes: If so, four people read on them, against the ברייתא.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאֵתוֹיֵי מַאי? לָאו לְאֵתוֹיֵי תַּעֲנִית צִיבּוּר וְתִשְׁעָה בְּאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב אשי's challenge by drawing out what the quoted כלל must mean.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling and the conclusion that three read on a תענית ציבור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A כלל written after explicit cases must include something more. The only candidates are a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב, so the משנה gives them four readers.

steps.title: If רב אשי is right, whose view is the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אשי. If the משנה requires four readers on a תענית ציבור, it matches neither the תנא קמא nor רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רב אשי, whose opinion is our משנה? It is not the תנא קמא and not רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks רב אשי's reading of the משנה. If he is right, the משנה would follow no known opinion. This step sets up a ברייתא that will prove the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said the כלל in our משנה adds four readers on a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב. The גמרא answers that every known תנא allows at most three readers on those days. So רב אשי's reading would leave our משנה with no author, which is a serious problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is it? (Whose opinion is this?)
The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה or ברייתא
A תנא who disagrees in the ברייתא about to be quoted

phrases.english: But according to Rav Ashi, whose view is our Mishnah?

phrases.aramaic: לָא תַּנָּא קַמָּא וְלָא רַבִּי יוֹסֵי,
phrases.english: It is neither the first Tanna nor Rabbi Yosei,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's objection with a counter-objection: his reading leaves the משנה without an author.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that 'זה הכלל' adds four readers on a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A reading of a משנה that matches no known תנא is unlikely. Every known view gives at most three readers on these days.

steps.title: The ברייתא about readers on תשעה באב
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא shows the two views on תשעה באב. Both allow at most three readers, so neither supports four.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: if תשעה באב falls on Monday or Thursday, three people read and one of them reads the הפטרה. If it falls on Tuesday or Wednesday, one person reads and that same person reads the הפטרה. רבי יוסי says: three people always read, and one of them reads the הפטרה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to prove the previous step. In it, two opinions argue about how many read on תשעה באב, and neither says four.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says three readers on Monday and Thursday, the regular Torah-reading days, and only one reader on other weekdays. רבי יוסי says three readers always. The two argue between one and three, but nobody says four, so רב אשי's reading of the משנה has no author.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught (in a ברייתא)
The one who reads the הפטרה, the reading from the Prophets
It happens to fall on (a certain day)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Three read and one is מפטיר' does not mean four people in total. The מפטיר is one of the three readers, as the Sefaria translation explains ('the last one of them concludes').

phrases.english: as it is taught: If it (Tisha B'Av) falls on Monday or Thursday,
three read, and one (of them) reads the haftara.
On Tuesday or Wednesday,
one reads, and that one reads the haftara.
Rabbi Yosei says:
Three always read, and one (of them) reads the haftara!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the claim in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that no תנא requires four readers on תשעה באב or a תענית ציבור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where the תנא קמא says one or three readers and רבי יוסי says always three.

steps.title: Then what does 'זה הכלל' add?
steps.stepSummary: If we reject רב אשי, his original question comes back: what does the משנה's כלל add?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, 'זה הכלל' is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that rejecting רב אשי brings back his question. The phrase 'זה הכלל' usually comes to add something new, so what does it add here?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל in a משנה is normally there to include cases the משנה did not name. If it does not add fast days, it seems to add nothing. So the גמרא must still find a purpose for it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is the rule', a phrase that usually adds unnamed cases

phrases.english: But then, 'This is the rule' is difficult!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having rejected רב אשי's reading, the גמרא returns to the problem he raised.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that only three read on a תענית ציבור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the כלל does not add fast days, it seems to have no purpose in the משנה.

steps.title: The כלל adds ראש חודש and חול המועד
steps.stepSummary: First answer: the כלל comes to include ראש חודש and חול המועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it comes to include ראש חודש and חול המועד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests the כלל adds ראש חודש and חול המועד, not fast days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These days have a מוסף and are not a יום טוב, so they fit the כלל exactly. That gives the כלל a job without adding four readers on fast days.

keyTerms.meaning: Here it means חול המועד, the middle days of a festival

phrases.english: No, it comes to include Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 by naming other days the כלל could include.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The כלל must add fast days, otherwise it does nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The כלל adds ראש חודש and חול המועד instead.

steps.title: But the משנה already names those days
steps.stepSummary: Challenge: the משנה already says outright that four read on ראש חודש and חול המועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה already teaches this outright: on ראשי חדשים and חול המועד, four people read!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer of step 9. The משנה already names ראש חודש and חול המועד, so the כלל cannot be needed to add them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל should add something not already stated. Since these days already appear by name in the משנה, the problem of step 8 comes back.

phrases.english: But it teaches this explicitly:
On Rosh Chodesh and Chol HaMoed, four read!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the כלל adds ראש חודש and חול המועד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These days are already named in the משנה, so a כלל adding them would be repetitive.

steps.title: The כלל is only a memory aid
steps.stepSummary: Final answer: the כלל adds no new days. It is a סימן that teaches the pattern: a day with more importance gets one extra reader.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is just giving a memory aid. Don't think that יום טוב and חול המועד are the same. Rather, hold this rule in your hand: whenever one day has more importance than another, it gets one extra reader.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the כלל does not add new days at all. It is a memory aid that explains the pattern behind the numbers of readers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The כלל does not add days. It shows the logic behind the numbers. Each step up in a day's importance adds one reader, so יום טוב gets more readers than חול המועד even though both are festival days. With this answer, רב אשי's objection falls away, and the ברייתא's ruling of three readers on a תענית ציבור stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Hold firmly in your hand (remember this)

steps.whatToRemember: 'זה הכלל' here is only a סימן: more importance means one more reader. It does not add fast days, so only three read on a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves the ruling of the ברייתא against רב אשי's objection. It also shows that a 'זה הכלל' in a משנה does not always add new cases; sometimes it only explains the pattern.

phrases.english: It merely gives a mnemonic,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא תֵּימָא יוֹם טוֹב וְחוּלּוֹ שֶׁל מוֹעֵד
phrases.english: so that you should not say that Yom Tov and Chol HaMoed
are the same as each other,
rather, hold this rule in your hand:
Any day that has an added element beyond its fellow,
gets an additional extra man.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by changing what the כלל is for, from adding cases to serving as a memory aid.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what the כלל is for (memory aid, not adding cases)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every 'זה הכלל' must add cases the משנה did not name.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here the כלל only teaches the pattern of the numbers: each step up in importance adds one reader.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב אשי's objection is answered. Only three read on a תענית ציבור and תשעה באב.

steps.title: The ladder of readers: four, five, six, seven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the סימן. Each step up in holiness adds one reader: ראש חודש and מועד get four, יום טוב five, יום הכפורים six, and שבת seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, on ראש חודש and חול המועד, which have a קרבן מוסף, four people read. On יום טוב, when work is forbidden, five. On יום הכפורים, where doing work is punished with כרת, six. On שבת, where doing work is punished with סקילה, seven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is filling in the details of the סימן it just explained in Step 11. It shows exactly which feature of each day earns it one more reader.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each level adds something more serious. First a קרבן מוסף, then a ban on work, then a ban whose punishment is כרת, then a ban whose punishment is סקילה. Each added level of seriousness adds exactly one reader. This is why the משנה's כלל adds no new days. It only teaches this pattern.

keyTerms.meaning: the additional offering brought on special days
stoning, the most severe court death penalty

steps.whatToRemember: More holiness means one more reader. ראש חודש and מועד: 4. יום טוב: 5. יום הכפורים: 6. שבת: 7.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the number of עליות we call up today on each kind of day.

phrases.english: Therefore, on the New Moon and the intermediate Festival days,
where there is an additional offering, four read.
phrases.notes: These days have a קרבן מוסף, but work is still allowed on them.

phrases.aramaic: בְּיוֹם טוֹב, דְּאָסוּר בַּעֲשִׂיַּית מְלָאכָה — חֲמִשָּׁה.
phrases.english: On a Festival, when doing work is forbidden: five.
On Yom Kippur, which is punished with karet: six.
Shabbat, where there is a prohibition punished by stoning: seven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the full sequence of the סימן given in Step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The number of readers rises by one with each level of holiness: 4, 5, 6, 7.

steps.title: The story of רב on a fast day in Babylonia
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to a story about רב. On a תענית צבור he read from the Torah, made a ברכה only at the start, and did not fall on his face when everyone else did.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the story itself: רב came to בבל on a public fast day. He got up and read from the Torah scroll. He made a ברכה at the beginning but not at the end. Everyone fell on their faces in prayer, but רב did not fall on his face.
steps.whatsHappening: The word גופה tells us the גמרא is going back to look closely at a story it mentioned earlier. This step sets up the questions that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story holds two strange details. First, רב made a ברכה at the start of his reading but not at the end. Second, he did not join everyone else in falling on his face. The next step asks about the second detail.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter itself: returning to examine something mentioned earlier
happened to come to a place
falling on the face, bowing down during the supplication prayers

steps.confusionAlert: Falling on the face here is not just leaning on your arm like we do today. In רב's time it meant bowing down low toward the floor.

phrases.english: The matter itself:
phrases.notes: Returning to a story quoted earlier in the sugya.

phrases.english: Rav happened to come to Babylonia on a public fast day,
he stood up and read from the Torah scroll.
At the start he made a blessing; at the end he did not make a blessing.
Everyone fell on their faces,
but Rav did not fall on his face.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of how many people read and goes back to examine an earlier story about רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב did not fall on his face on the fast day, while everyone else did.

steps.title: Why didn't רב bow down?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב did not fall on his face like everyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason רב did not fall on his face?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the story: why did רב act differently from everyone else? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone else was following the normal practice. So רב, a great Torah leader, must have had a special reason to hold back. The גמרא wants to know what it was.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא רַב לָא נְפַל עַל אַפֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: What is the reason Rav did not fall on his face?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא רַב לָא נְפַל עַל אַפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the unusual behavior described in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason רב did not bow down with everyone else.

steps.title: Bowing on a stone floor is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The floor was made of stone. The Torah forbids bowing down on a stone floor anywhere except the בית המקדש. As עולא says, the ban applies only to a stone floor.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was a stone floor. A ברייתא teaches about the פסוק: "Do not place a figured stone in your land to bow down on it." On it you may not bow down in your land, but you may bow down on the stones of the בית המקדש. This follows עולא, who said: the Torah only forbade bowing on a stone floor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רב did not bow down because the floor was stone, and bowing down on stone outside the בית המקדש is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the פסוק that bowing down on stone is forbidden outside the בית המקדש, but allowed inside it. עולא makes the ban narrower: it covers only a stone floor, not other surfaces. Since this floor was stone, רב held back.

keyTerms.meaning: a figured or decorated stone (ויקרא כו:א)
an אמורא who limits the ban to a stone floor only

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of not bowing on a bare stone floor outside the מקדש. Some people cover the floor when bowing on יום כיפור because of it.

phrases.english: It was a stone floor,
and it was taught in a baraita:
"Nor shall you place a figured stone in your land
to bow down upon it."
"Upon it" you may not bow down in your land,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אַתָּה מִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה עַל אֲבָנִים שֶׁל בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
phrases.english: but you may bow down on the stones of the Temple.
This follows Ulla,
as Ulla said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אָסְרָה תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא רִצְפָּה שֶׁל אֲבָנִים בִּלְבָד.
phrases.english: The Torah forbade only a stone floor.
phrases.notes: Bowing on other surfaces, such as dirt, is not included in this ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The floor was stone, and the Torah forbids bowing on a stone floor outside the בית המקדש.

steps.title: Then why only רב?
steps.stepSummary: If the floor was stone, everyone else should not have bowed either. Why does the story single out רב?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why mention רב specifically? Everyone else should also not have bowed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. If a stone floor is the problem, the ban should apply to the whole congregation, not just to רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on stone is a law for everyone, not just a special practice for רב. So the answer seems to prove too much. It cannot explain why only רב held back while everyone else bowed.

phrases.english: If so, why specifically Rav?
All of them too should not have bowed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that רב held back because of the stone floor.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah ban on bowing on stone would apply to the whole congregation, yet they all bowed.

steps.title: The stone was only in front of רב
steps.stepSummary: Only the part of the floor in front of רב was stone. The rest of the floor was not, so the others were allowed to bow.
steps.simpleTranslation: The stone floor was only in front of רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Only the spot where רב stood was paved with stone, so only he had a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law stays the same for everyone. What was different was the floor. The others stood on an unpaved floor, where bowing is allowed. רב stood on the one stone section.
steps.whatToRemember: רב did not bow because the floor in front of him was stone, and bowing on a stone floor outside the מקדש is forbidden. The others stood where there was no stone.

phrases.english: It was only in front of Rav.
phrases.notes: Only the section of floor where רב stood was paved with stone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole floor was stone, so everyone should have held back.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the section in front of רב was stone, so only he could not bow.

steps.title: Why didn't רב just move to where the people were?
steps.stepSummary: If only the floor in front of רב was stone, he should have walked over to the people and fallen on his face there.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him go over to the congregation and fall on his face there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. If the problem was only the stone in front of רב, he could easily have moved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 said only רב's spot was stone. That answer seems to create a simple fix: רב could step onto the non-stone floor. So why did he skip נפילת אפים completely?

keyTerms.meaning: And let him fall on his face

phrases.english: So let him go over to the congregation
and fall on his face there!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיזִיל לְגַבֵּי צִיבּוּרָא וְלִינְפּוֹל עַל אַפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 17 (only רב's spot was stone).
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that only the floor in front of רב was stone.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the problem was only where he stood, he could have moved and avoided it. Skipping נפילת אפים entirely makes no sense.

steps.title: He did not want to bother the people
steps.stepSummary: רב did not move because he did not want to trouble the congregation to make room for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did not want to trouble the congregation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Moving over would have forced the people to squeeze together to make space for רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer gives a practical, considerate reason. רב preferred to skip נפילת אפים rather than make everyone shift around for him.

phrases.english: He did not want to trouble the congregation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a practical reason why the obvious fix was not used.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב could easily have moved to non-stone floor, so his not bowing seems unexplained.
steps.terutzMaskana: Moving would have troubled the people, so רב chose not to.

steps.title: A second answer: רב bowed fully stretched out, unlike the others
steps.stepSummary: A different answer: רב's way of bowing was to stretch out his hands and feet completely. עולא says only that full stretching out is forbidden on stone. So the others, who only bent over, were allowed, and רב was not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say this instead: רב used to bow by stretching out his hands and feet. This follows עולא, because עולא said: The Torah forbade only stretching out the hands and feet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to answer the question of step 16, why everyone else could bow and רב could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the whole floor may be stone. The difference is in how people bowed. The others only bent over, which is allowed on stone. רב lay fully stretched out, which עולא says is the only thing the Torah forbids on stone.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces another answer
Stretching out the hands and feet: lying fully flat on the ground

steps.confusionAlert: In step 15 עולא's rule was about the floor (only stone is forbidden). Here a second statement of עולא is about the body position (only full stretching out is forbidden). Both limits apply together: the ban is full stretching out, on stone.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:

phrases.aramaic: רַב פִּישּׁוּט יָדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם הֲוָה עָבֵיד,
phrases.english: Rav used to stretch out his hands and feet,
phrases.notes: He lay fully flat, while the others only bent over.

phrases.english: and this follows Ulla.
For Ulla said:
The Torah did not forbid
anything except stretching out the hands and feet alone.
phrases.notes: That is, bowing on a stone floor.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: רַב פִּישּׁוּט יָדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם הֲוָה עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to step 16, replacing the 'only his spot was stone' answer of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the people by how they bowed, not by where they stood.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the floor was stone, everyone's bowing should have been forbidden equally.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only full stretching out on stone is forbidden. רב bowed that way, so he could not. The others only bent over, so they could.

steps.title: Why didn't רב just bow without stretching out?
steps.stepSummary: If simple bowing is allowed on stone, רב should have fallen on his face the simple way, like everyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him fall on his face without stretching out his hands and feet!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second answer. If only full stretching out is forbidden, רב had an easy option: bow the allowed way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said the problem was רב's style of bowing. But style can be changed. So why skip נפילת אפים instead of doing it the permitted way?

phrases.english: So let him fall on his face,
and not stretch out his hands and feet!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיפּוֹל עַל אַפֵּיהּ, וְלָא לֶיעְבֵּיד פִּישּׁוּט יָדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second answer given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רב's full stretching out was the problem.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An allowed form of bowing existed, so רב could have used it instead of not bowing at all.

steps.title: רב would not change his custom
steps.stepSummary: רב did not want to change his usual way of bowing. Since he could not do it his way on stone, he did not bow at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would not change his custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: רב kept his personal custom of bowing fully.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's custom was always full stretching out. He preferred not to bow at all rather than bow in a lesser way. So on the stone floor he simply did not fall on his face.

phrases.english: He would not change from his custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 and closes the second answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the permitted option was not used: personal custom.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב could have bowed the simple, permitted way.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב did not change his custom of full bowing, so on stone he skipped bowing.

steps.title: A third answer: an important person is different
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: רב was an important person. רבי אלעזר says an important person should not fall on his face in public unless he is sure his prayer will be answered, like יהושע בן נון.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say this instead: an important person is different, following רבי אלעזר. For רבי אלעזר said: An important person may not fall on his face unless he will be answered like יהושע בן נון, as it says: 'And ה׳ said to יהושע: Get up.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a completely new answer to the original question of step 14. This answer has nothing to do with the stone floor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When יהושע fell on his face, ה׳ answered him right away and told him to get up. A great person who falls on his face in public and is not answered would be shamed. So רב, an important person, did not fall on his face.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא gives three explanations for why רב did not fall on his face. First, only his spot was stone, and he did not want to trouble the people by moving. Second, he always bowed fully stretched out, which is forbidden on stone, and he would not change his custom. Third, an important person should not fall on his face in public unless he will be answered like יהושע.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the idea that a distinguished person must be careful with public acts of prayer, so that an unanswered prayer does not cause disgrace.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
an important person is different,
following Rabbi Elazar.
For Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אָדָם חָשׁוּב רַשַּׁאי לִיפּוֹל עַל פָּנָיו
phrases.english: An important person is not permitted to fall on his face
phrases.notes: In public.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נַעֲנֶה כִּיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן,
phrases.english: unless he will be answered like Joshua bin Nun,
as it is written:
"And ה׳ said to Joshua: Get up, etc."
phrases.notes: יהושע ז:י. ה׳ answered יהושע's falling on his face right away.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אָדָם חָשׁוּב שָׁאנֵי, כִּדְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stone-floor discussion and gives a new answer to the original question of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the case through the status of the person, not the floor.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב should have fallen on his face like everyone else.
steps.terutzMaskana: As an important person, רב should not fall on his face in public unless he is sure to be answered like יהושע.

steps.title: Three kinds of bowing: קידה, כריעה, השתחואה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא defines three words for bowing, each with a פסוק. קידה is bowing with the face to the ground. כריעה is kneeling on the knees. השתחואה is lying fully stretched out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: קידה means on the face, as it says, 'בת שבע bowed with her face to the ground.' כריעה means on the knees, as it says, 'from kneeling on his knees.' השתחואה means stretching out the hands and feet, as it says, 'Shall I and your mother and your brothers come to bow down to you to the ground?'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the discussion was about kinds of bowing, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that defines the three main Hebrew words for bowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word gets its own meaning and a proof from a פסוק. בת שבע's face touched the ground (קידה). שלמה knelt on his knees (כריעה). In יוסף's dream the family bows 'to the ground', meaning fully stretched out (השתחואה). This explains the full stretching out that רב did.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
Bowing with the face toward the ground
Full prostration, with hands and feet stretched out
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: קידה means face to the ground. כריעה means on the knees. השתחואה means fully stretched out.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Kidda means on the face,
as it says: "And Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground."
phrases.notes: I Kings 1:31.

phrases.english: Keria means on the knees,
and so it says: "from kneeling on his knees."
phrases.notes: מלכים א ח:נד, about שלמה.

phrases.english: Hishtachava'a means stretching out the hands and feet,
as it says:
"Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come
to bow down to you to the ground?"
phrases.notes: בראשית לז:י, יעקב's reaction to יוסף's dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leads on from the talk of רב's full stretching out to a general definition of the kinds of bowing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קידה is face to the ground, כריעה is on the knees, and השתחואה is full stretching out of hands and feet, each proven from a פסוק.

steps.title: לוי demonstrates קידה and becomes lame
steps.stepSummary: לוי showed רבי how קידה is done and was injured. He became lame.
steps.simpleTranslation: לוי demonstrated קידה in front of רבי, and he became lame.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story that shows how hard קידה is. לוי tried to demonstrate it for רבי and hurt himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קידה was just defined as bowing with the face to the ground. According to the classic explanation, it meant bending all the way down onto the thumbs and coming right back up, which is very demanding physically. The story proves how hard it was: even a great person like לוי was injured doing it.

keyTerms.meaning: bowing with the face to the ground
in front of רבי (רבי יהודה הנשיא)
became lame, was injured in the leg or hip

phrases.english: Levi demonstrated kidda
phrases.notes: He showed how the bowing called קידה is done.

phrases.english: before Rabbi, and he became lame.
phrases.notes: The physical strain injured him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how hard the קידה just defined in the ברייתא really is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קידה is so hard that לוי was injured demonstrating it.

steps.title: Was it really the bowing that made Levi lame?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the story. רבי אלעזר says לוי became lame because he spoke harshly toward Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was it this bowing that caused his injury? But רבי אלעזר said: A person should never speak harshly toward Heaven, because a great man once spoke harshly toward Heaven and became lame. Who was he? לוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story by quoting רבי אלעזר. רבי אלעזר gives a different reason for לוי's lameness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There seem to be two different explanations for one injury. The story blames the physical effort of קידה. רבי אלעזר blames a spiritual cause: לוי spoke boldly to ה׳ in a prayer for rain, as told in תענית. So which one is the real cause?

phrases.english: And was it this that caused it for him?
phrases.notes: Was the bowing really the cause of the injury?

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Elazar say:
A person should never speak harshly
words toward Heaven,
for a great man spoke harshly
words toward Heaven and became lame
and who was he? Levi.
phrases.notes: The story of his bold prayer appears in תענית 25a.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא גְּרַמָא לֵיהּ? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the cause of the injury given in the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that demonstrating קידה made לוי lame.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר says a different cause, speaking harshly toward Heaven, made לוי lame. That contradicts the story.

steps.title: Both causes together made him lame
steps.stepSummary: Both things caused it. His harsh words made him deserve punishment, and the punishment came through the bowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: This and that both caused it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that both explanations are true at once. There is no contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The harsh words were the spiritual reason לוי deserved to be hurt. The hard bowing was the physical way the injury actually happened. So one explanation gives the reason and the other gives the means.

phrases.english: This and that caused it for him.
phrases.notes: The words made him deserve punishment, and the bowing was how it happened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by combining both causes.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: both causes are true together.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only one cause can be the real one, so the story and רבי אלעזר disagree.
steps.terutzMaskana: The harsh words made him deserve punishment, and the strain of קידה was the means of the injury.
steps.whatToRemember: קידה was physically very hard. לוי's injury came from both his harsh words toward Heaven and the strain of the bowing.

steps.title: רב חייא בר אבין begins a report about how אביי bowed
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין begins describing how he saw אביי bow. The report continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אבין said: I saw אביי...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. רב חייא בר אבין starts a firsthand report about how the חכמים bowed, and the rest of his statement continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic of bowing is still going, but now the גמרא turns to an eyewitness account of real practice. This is only the opening line, so the actual information has not come yet.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who reports what he saw

phrases.english: Rav Chiya bar Avin said:
I saw them, Abaye
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין: חֲזֵינָא לְהוּ לְאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from לוי's story to an eyewitness report of how the חכמים actually bowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not complete yet. The report of how אביי bowed continues on the next amud.
